claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by competition between thermally activated dislocation glide and the formation of deformation twins or stacking faults.
Deformation twins and stacking faults act as barriers to dislocation motion in FeNiCrMn.
Temperature and strain rate modulate the competition between dislocation glide and secondary-feature formation.
The competition between these deformation modes maintains the strength–ductility balance of FeNiCrMn.
Higher temperatures and lower strain rates favor thermally activated dislocation glide.
Higher temperatures and lower strain rates favor the formation of deformation twins or stacking faults in FeNiCrMn.
Twins or stacking faults enhance ductility by impeding rapid slip.
Lower temperatures or high strain rates suppress deformation twins and stacking faults.
When secondary deformation features are suppressed, plasticity relies mainly on dislocation glide.
Suppression of secondary deformation features increases yield strength at the expense of ductility.
Moderate strain rates and elevated temperatures will produce a balanced strength–ductility profile.
The balanced strength–ductility profile at moderate strain rates and elevated temperatures will coincide with observable deformation twins or stacking faults.
Low temperatures or high strain rates will produce higher yield strength and reduced ductility.
The deformed microstructure at low temperatures or high strain rates will be dominated by dislocation glide.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to single-phase Co-free FeNiCrMn with a controlled microstructure.
Phase transformations, secondary-phase precipitation, or significant grain-structure changes may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
